items.prompt: Which of these is the strongest anchor term for a phone problem?
choices: The words "phone" and "problem" together
The phone's exact model plus the message on its screen
The words "help" and "fix" typed at the front of the query
items.explanation: A model and an exact message appear only in sources about your case.

items.prompt: What is an anchor term?
choices: A specific word that appears mostly in sources about your case
The first word you type into any search box
A word that makes the search engine respond much more quickly
items.explanation: Anchors are specific enough to rule out unrelated sources.

items.prompt: Why did the librarian find the right book after the second ask?
choices: The librarian listened more carefully the second time
The library had added many new books during the minutes between asks
The ask carried specifics only one kind of book could match
items.explanation: Age and topic detail pointed at a small set of books.

items.prompt: In "[router model] intermittent disconnect", what do the square brackets mean?
choices: Type the brackets exactly as written
Replace it with the model printed on your router
Leave that part out and search with the other words
items.explanation: It is a placeholder for your own detail.

items.prompt: Which query is vaguer?
choices: "Northfield High transfer form 2025"
"Northfield High transfer form deadline"
"school form"
items.explanation: Only the first lacks a school, form name and year.

items.prompt: What happens to results when you add a truly specific term?
choices: Most remaining results are ruled out
A few extra results are added
The same results appear in a new order
items.explanation: Sources must match every term, so specific terms remove many.

items.prompt: Which of these makes a poor anchor term?
choices: An exact error message
The word "broken"
A software version number
items.explanation: "Broken" fits nearly every complaint ever posted.

items.prompt: The first search was called vague. What was wrong with it?
choices: The search engine was not working properly
It was typed with far too many long and awkward words
Its words fit thousands of unrelated problems
items.explanation: Generic words cannot point at one situation.

items.prompt: Jordan adds the word "issue" and the word "fix" to "wifi keeps disconnecting". Why does the list barely shrink?
choices: Search engines ignore any word shorter than six letters
Each added word is counted as a single repeated term
Both words appear in nearly every troubleshooting post
The engine only reads the first three words typed
items.explanation: Generic words are matched by almost every source, so they filter almost nothing.
items.reference:
Vague word or anchor?
❌ "problem", "help", "broken": matched by almost everything
✅ Model number, exact error text, version: matched by few sources
🔍 A source must match every term to appear
Why: a specific term can only appear in sources about your case, so each one removes most of what is left.
items.learnMore:
Anchor terms narrow because sources must match all of them

A generic word is shared by nearly every source, so it filters nothing. A model number, an exact message or a version is shared by few, so each one removes most remaining results, and several together compound.

Common mistake

Adding more generic words ("help", "fix", "issue") and expecting the list to shrink.
items.reflection: Think of the last time you asked a person for help and got a shrug. What detail could you have added that only your situation has?

items.explanation: 42,000 / 10 = 4,200, then 4,200 / 10 = 420. This is an assumed model, not a measurement.

items.prompt: What is the main job of the first search in the loop?
choices: Find the final answer on the first page
Gather better terms for the next search
Prove that the topic is too hard to search
items.explanation: Skimming for terms is the point of a first pass.

items.prompt: When you skim results, what are you mainly looking for?
choices: The result with the longest description
The pages that show the most advertisements per screen
Model numbers and wording that repeat across results
items.explanation: Repeated specific words become your next anchors.

items.prompt: Which part of a result do you skim?
choices: The title, snippet, site name and date
Every paragraph of every page listed
Only the comments at the very bottom
items.explanation: Skimming uses the visible clues, not full reading.

items.prompt: After a failed first search, what is the best next step?
choices: Give up because the answer cannot exist
Search again using terms the results revealed
Type the very same words again but more slowly
items.explanation: The loop feeds new terms into a new search.

items.prompt: What did Jordan's first search teach?
choices: That the router was too old to fix
That Wi-Fi problems have no causes
The router model and the word "firmware"
items.explanation: Those two words became search 2's anchors.

items.prompt: If three results use a word you do not know, what might it be?
choices: A mistake that all three sites made
Vocabulary your next query needs
A word to avoid in every search
items.explanation: Repeated unfamiliar terms are often the field's own words.

items.prompt: How many times does the loop run?
choices: Until the answer appears or one source is clear
Exactly twice, no more and no less
Once for each word in the original query
items.explanation: It repeats until a stopping condition is met.

items.prompt: What does "firmware" mean in Jordan's story?
choices: The metal case around the router
The cable that connects to the wall
The router's built-in software
items.explanation: It is the software stored inside the device.

items.prompt: Search 1 returned forum chatter, but one reply named a model and a fault. What should Jordan do with that reply?
choices: Follow its advice immediately without searching further
Reuse its model and fault wording as anchors in a new search
Ignore it because replies in forums are never useful to anyone
Copy the whole reply into the search box unchanged
items.explanation: Its specific terms are the scouting result; the new search tests them properly.
items.reference:
Search, skim, refine
🔎 Search with the best terms you have
👀 Skim titles and snippets for better terms
🔁 Search again with those terms as anchors
🛑 Stop when the answer appears or one source is clear
Why: a first search that fails still tells you which words the next one should use.
items.learnMore:
The first search is scouting

Skimming is not reading everything. It means picking up model numbers, exact wording and the vocabulary people close to the problem use, then feeding them back in as anchors.

Common mistake

Treating a poor first result set as proof that the answer is not out there.
items.reflection: Recall a time a failed attempt taught you what to ask next. What did it reveal that you could not have known at the start?

Neither, because the loop forbids skimming results
The second, who picked up terms from the results
Both, because each of them searched more than once
items.explanation: The loop's refine step needs new terms; repeating the same words adds nothing.

items.prompt: Which question is best answered by going straight to a source?
choices: How do most people feel about this app?
What does this app's setting actually do?
What is a fun app to try next?
items.explanation: A question about the tool itself is best settled by its own docs.

items.prompt: Why are forum threads weaker than official documentation on a tool's exact behavior?
choices: They are always written by beginners
They are never available at the moment you need them
They add guessing on top of the original
items.explanation: Each retelling is a layer where errors can enter.

items.prompt: Results keep linking back to one page. What should you do?
choices: Read only the pages that link to it
Read that page directly
Close the search and start over
items.explanation: A page everyone cites is the source.

items.prompt: Which is an example of a primary source?
choices: A manufacturer's support page
A blog post summarizing that page
A video guessing at the cause
items.explanation: The maker's own page is the original.

items.prompt: Does "official" mean always right for your case?
choices: Yes, nothing official can ever be outdated
Yes, but only when the page is read on a weekday
No, check that it matches your version and date
items.explanation: Official pages can be old or for another model.

items.prompt: When is broad searching fine?
choices: When you need a product's exact warranty terms
When you want general experiences with something
When one office published the rule you need
items.explanation: Opinions and experiences are spread across many places.

items.prompt: Which source would know if an app is down?
choices: A forum thread from last year
A friend's guess on social media
The service's own status page
items.explanation: The status page is kept by those who see the system.

items.prompt: What do blogs summarizing a manual add?
choices: A layer where mistakes can enter
Information the manual does not have
A guarantee that the details are current
items.explanation: Summaries can be wrong or outdated.

items.prompt: You need the exact refund window for a product. Searches return posts from customers recalling "about a month". Best move?
choices: Average the customers' guesses and trust the result
Search for newer posts that repeat the same number again
Ask the first forum poster to confirm the number
Find the seller's own refund policy page and read it
items.explanation: The seller's policy settles it; recollections are secondhand.
items.reference:
Where does the answer live?
🌐 "What do people generally think?": broad search
📄 "What does this tool say?": its own documentation
🔗 Results all link to one page: that page is the source
⚠️ Still check version, country and date
Why: the maker or owner removes the layers of summary and guessing that can add errors.
items.learnMore:
Go to the source when the question is about the source

Documentation, changelogs, support pages and the text of a rule are written by whoever can settle the question. Secondary posts add summary and speculation on top.

Common mistake

Assuming an official page is always correct for you without checking its version, date and region.
items.reflection: Where in your own life do you rely on retellings when the original is easy to read? What might a retelling have changed?

Wait for a forum post to translate it for you

items.prompt: What is a primary source?
choices: The original place that can settle a claim
Any page ranked first by a search engine
A summary written by a helpful stranger online
items.explanation: Primary sources are original and authoritative.

items.prompt: What is a secondary source?
choices: The maker's own official page
The product's printed label and instruction leaflet
Someone describing or guessing from outside
items.explanation: Secondary sources report on the original.

items.prompt: The maker's page is gone. What question replaces "where is the answer"?
choices: How do I make the missing page come back?
Which outside reports can I trust?
Why did the maker remove it?
items.explanation: Trust becomes the problem when no original exists.

items.prompt: One forum user claims a fix works. How should you treat it?
choices: As settled fact, because it was posted
As false, because only one person said it
As a lead worth checking against others
items.explanation: One unverified claim is not yet evidence.

items.prompt: Which evidence is stronger?
choices: Three unrelated users reporting the same fix
One user repeating the same fix three times in a row
A single very long and detailed post
items.explanation: Independent agreement is harder to explain away.

items.prompt: What should independent reports share to count?
choices: The same username on different sites
The same model and the same symptom
The same posting time each day
items.explanation: Matching model and symptom make them comparable.

items.prompt: What was special about Jordan's maker page?
choices: It was the longest page in the results
It was written by another router owner
It was a primary source that could confirm the bug
items.explanation: The maker could settle the claim directly.

items.prompt: Where does deeper checking of secondary sources belong?
choices: Nowhere, since sources are not checked
Source evaluation, a related unit
Only inside the first search query
items.explanation: The unit points to source evaluation for this skill.

items.prompt: A discontinued heater has no manual online. Three people on different sites report the same cleaning step fixing the same model. Best reading?
choices: Proof that the fix works on every heater
Worthless, because none is the maker
Reasonable to try, with a safe way to undo it
Reliable only if all three use the same wording
items.explanation: Independent matching reports on one model raise trust but do not equal a maker's confirmation.
items.reference:
No maker page? Weigh the reports
🏛️ Primary: the original that can settle the claim
💬 Secondary: someone describing or guessing
👥 Independent reports on the same model count for more
1️⃣ One unverified post is a lead, not a fact
Why: without a primary source, trust comes from several independent, matching reports.
items.learnMore:
When the original is gone, count independent matches

Several unrelated people reporting the same symptom on the same model with the same fix is stronger evidence than one claim, because they did not copy each other.

Common mistake

Counting reposts or quotes of one claim as if each were a separate, independent report.
items.reflection: Think of a claim you once accepted from a single person. What would several independent confirmations have looked like?

Happening only once and never again
Happening, stopping, then coming back
items.explanation: Intermittent problems appear and disappear.

items.prompt: What does "packet loss" mean in plain terms?
choices: Small pieces of internet traffic fail to arrive
The internet bill was not paid on time
A router was physically lost or stolen
items.explanation: Packets are the small pieces data travels in.

Experts write using their field's specific terms
Everyday words are always misspelled online

items.prompt: What is the first search's job when you lack the vocabulary?
choices: To find the final answer at once
To prove the topic has no name
To surface the field's own words

items.prompt: Do you need technical vocabulary before you start searching?

No, you can pick it up from the first results

items.explanation: The loop is designed to discover vocabulary.

items.prompt: Which phrase is more likely to match a diagnosis page?
choices: "intermittent packet loss"
"internet goes weird sometimes"
"things keep stopping now and then"
items.explanation: The field's term matches specialists' pages.

items.prompt: Which describes the vocabulary step?
choices: A separate method unrelated to the loop
A step done only after finding the answer
The refinement loop started one level earlier
items.explanation: It is the same loop aimed at vocabulary.

items.prompt: What do you do with a term you meet in results?
choices: Delete it, since you did not choose it
Try it as an anchor in the next search
Avoid it until you can define it exactly
items.explanation: New terms become your next anchors.

items.prompt: You search "my screen goes black for a moment" and find results vague and mixed. Several good pages say "intermittent display dropout". Best next query?
choices: Repeat the original wording with more emphasis
Add "please help" so replies seem more urgent
Remove every technical-sounding word from the query before searching
Include "intermittent display dropout" plus your device model
items.explanation: The field's phrase plus your model gives sharp anchors.
items.reference:
Everyday words vs the field's words
🗣️ "internet keeps stopping for a second": everyday, vague results
🔧 "intermittent packet loss": the field's term, sharp results
🧭 First search: collect the field's words
🎯 Second search: use them as anchors
Why: people who diagnose a problem name it in specific vocabulary, so those words match their pages.

Casual wording is always rejected by diagnostic sites

items.prompt: Someone says they cannot search until they learn the technical terms. What does the unit's method suggest?
choices: They are right, so study a textbook before searching
They should ask a friend to type the query
They should wait until the problem fully disappears
Search plainly first and learn the terms from the results
items.explanation: The first search exists to supply the vocabulary.
items.reference:
Everyday words vs the field's words
🗣️ "internet keeps stopping for a second": everyday, vague results
🔧 "intermittent packet loss": the field's term, sharp results
🧭 First search: collect the field's words
🎯 Second search: use them as anchors
Why: people who diagnose a problem name it in specific vocabulary, so those words match their pages.
items.learnMore:
The first search can supply the vocabulary

You do not need the field's words to begin. Describe it plainly, skim for the terms experts keep using, and let those words become the anchors.
